The Commons Fridge2026MA final project

Make shared care easier to negotiate.

Five habit interviews redirected a full-inventory concept toward lighter shared coordination: see the item, understand ownership, then decide what can be done.

Problem
In a shared flat, the trouble with one fridge is not only forgotten food: people hesitate to remind each other, the same person ends up tidying, and nobody is sure whose things can be touched.
Key decisions
I dropped the full-inventory idea and designed for four moments only: putting something in, checking and handling, before shopping, and finding something. Where an item is, whose it is and what others may do are three separate things; an unclaimed item stays “not sure whose”.
Outcome
A working bilingual prototype, and NFC entry points on the fridge door.
Context
University of Southampton · MA final project
My role
Research, system design, interactions & prototype
Period
2026
Delivery
Physical touchpoints, bilingual prototype & demonstration

01 · Research

The friction is social as well as practical.

I conducted five interviews about existing shared-fridge habits. The problems went beyond forgotten items: hesitation about reminding someone, recurring care work falling to one person, and repeated conflict around unclear boundaries.

U02 worried that a group message could sound like a complaint; U01 carried the work of checking and organising; U05 described how boundaries and capacity pressure affected participation.

Tobie’s note

Make the next shared action clearer without turning a reminder into a public record of who failed.

02 · Reframing

Reduce the burden instead of building a bigger inventory.

A complete inventory depends on people continually entering and maintaining information. That can add work for the person already doing the organising. I shifted toward moments that need coordination: putting something in, checking or handling it, shopping and moving out.

Put in

Declare a plan

Capture the chosen plan rather than demand a complete inventory.

Check

See what needs attention

Group by area rather than attaching a problem label to a person.

Coordinate

Respect ownership

Seeing an item does not give someone permission to dispose of it.

03 · From findings to features

Every feature walks back to a behaviour someone described.

After coding the five interviews into behaviour cards, I identified nine ways a shared fridge fails (FP1–FP9). Each is a pattern seen across interviews rather than a single anecdote, and each names the interviews that produced it, so it can be checked.

Each feature in the build answers one of them. FP2 — identical packaging with no owner occupying space for months — became a found-something entry that locks ownership to unknown with a 48-hour hold. FP9 — a user withdrawing to avoid conflict — became a four-step move-out handover.

Tobie’s note

If a feature cannot be walked back, I mark it as a design judgement rather than a finding.

04 · Interaction rules

Location, ownership and permission are separate.

I separated where an item is, who claims it and what someone else may do with it. Unclaimed items retain unknown ownership. Neither a location nor a photograph automatically establishes an owner or permission to act.

The House view groups items by area, not by person. The character describes situations without judging people. The interface does not determine food safety; judgement and action remain with the person.

05 · Physical & digital

Put the entry where the action happens.

Add and Manage are two clear entry points on the fridge door: record an intention when putting something away, or review what is already there. NFC links and a QR fallback connect the physical prompt to the detailed phone flow.

The penguin gives reminders a caring tone. I used AI-assisted visual iteration, then selected and refined a consistent character system.

The character was iterated with a generative image tool. The written specification came before the images, and each round rewrote the prompt rather than re-rolling the same one. The first two rounds were refused outright — one reason on record is that they read as generic AI mascot art — and the flat fourth round was carried into the expression system and the printed pieces. Because the specification came first, refusing a render was a documented decision rather than a matter of taste.

06 · Prototype & outcome

From a tap on the fridge door to a confirmed plan.

The submitted v1.7 functional prototype brings seven routes and both languages into one page; the one embedded below is v1.8, updated for the exhibition. A researcher demonstration documents the sequence of touching the entry, working with an item, entering details and confirming a plan.

The next step is to put this journey in front of participants; the test materials are ready — see the next section.

07 · Next iteration

Observe use before claiming effectiveness.

The next iteration would test whether first-time users understand the plan-based framing, then compare character directions and NFC entry points. The comparison kit is ready; testing will run under an appropriate research scope and consent process.

I would also seek a household that successfully maintains a shared inventory. The existing sample describes failure more fully; a counterexample could clarify which complexity is useful and which can be removed.
